title: Sprint 1, task 3: Find what customers mean
where: This is the heart of AskMate: finding the right product however a customer asks.
next: Go back to the portal. Your checks are running.

steps.title: Customers ask in their own words
steps.body:
Real customers never type a product code. They say rimless toilet, commode or 18 by 14 basin. Today AskMate says no to all of them.
Do this. Click the button and read what each customer wanted.

steps.title: How AskMate will find products
steps.body:
You did this for dishes in Mission 4. Now you do it for 35 products, in search.py:
1. words(text) turns a question into clean words, and drops small words like do and the.
2. SYNONYMS turns a customer's word into the word the list uses: commode becomes toilet.
3. score(asked, product) counts how many of the customer's words describe a product.
4. find keeps the products with the best score. Then AskMate answers if there is one, asks which one if there are a few, and says no if there are none.
Steps 1 to 3 have a Try it table: all green means done. Step 4 is done when the customers are happy.

steps.title: Predict first
steps.body:
How many words do these two sets share?
{"rimless", "toilet"} & {"lexo", "one", "piece", "toilet", "rimless"}
steps.explain: & keeps the words that are in both sets. That count is exactly the score you will write.

steps.title: Turn a question into clean words
steps.body: The problem. toilet? with a question mark never equals toilet, and 18 by 14 is three words, not one size.
hints: Do it in the order of the list. Sizes first, before the spaces are gone.
lower(), then replace(" by ", "x") and replace(" x ", "x"). A loop replaces each mark with a space. A list comprehension keeps the words not in STOPWORDS.
Nearly there:  text = text.lower().replace(" by ", "x").replace(" x ", "x")  ,  for mark in "?!.,()": text = text.replace(mark, " ")  , then  return [w for w in text.split() if w not in ____]

answer.why: Sizes are joined first, while 18 and 14 still have spaces around by. Each mark becomes a space, so (18x14x7 inch) splits into clean words. The list comprehension keeps only the words that tell you something.

steps.well_done: Every question is clean words now, and so is every product.

args: Do you have a rimless toilet?

steps.ask: Make words turn a sentence into clean words that AskMate can compare.
steps.gets: a question or a product's text, like "Do you have a rimless toilet?"
steps.gives: a list of the useful words: ["rimless", "toilet"]
approach: Join sizes while they still have spaces: replace " by " and " x " with "x", so 18 by 14 becomes 18x14.
Replace each of ? ! . , ( ) with a space.
Split into words, and keep only the words that are not in STOPWORDS (small words like do, the and have).
steps.done: every row of the Try it table is green.

steps.title: Teach AskMate the words customers use
steps.body: The problem. Customers say commode, WC or faucet. HomeShine's list only says toilet and tap.
hints: A dictionary maps one thing to another, like {"key": "value"}. Look at the table: which words must become which?
You need commode and wc to become toilet, and faucet and taps to become tap. Plurals help too: toilets, basins, sinks.

answer.why: meaning(word) looks the word up in SYNONYMS. If it is there, it gives the list's word; if not, it gives the word back unchanged, so basin stays basin.

steps.well_done: AskMate speaks the customers' language now.
steps.ask: Fill the SYNONYMS dictionary, so a customer's word becomes the word HomeShine's list uses.
steps.gets: a customer's word, like "commode" (the function meaning looks it up for you)
steps.gives: the list's word: "toilet". A word that is not in the dictionary comes back unchanged.
approach: Look at the Try it table: which words must become which?
Each key is a customer's word, and each value is the list's word: "commode": "toilet".
Add the plurals too: toilets, taps, basins and sinks.
Keep the whole dictionary on one line, then save.
steps.where: search.py, the line SYNONYMS = {}. Leave meaning alone: it already uses your dictionary.
steps.done: every row of the Try it table is green.

steps.title: Score each product
steps.body: The problem. To find the best product, AskMate needs a number for how well each product matches.
hints: You predicted this a few steps ago. Which operator keeps only what two sets share?
Turn asked into a set, use & with product_words(product), and count what is left with len().

answer.why: set(asked) & product_words(product) keeps the words found in both, and len() counts them. Two shared words score 2, so a better match always scores higher.

steps.well_done: Every product gets a score for every question.
steps.ask: Make score count how many of the customer's words describe one product.
steps.gets: the customer's words, like ["rimless", "toilet"], and one product
steps.gives: a number: 2 for Lexo (it is rimless and a toilet), 1 for Glanza (only a toilet), 0 for no match
approach: product_words(product) already gives you the product's words, as a set.
Make a set of the customer's words too: set(asked).
& keeps only the words that are in both sets. You predicted this a few steps ago.
Count what is left with len(), and return it.
steps.where: search.py, the function score. It needs only one line.
steps.done: every row of the Try it table is green.

steps.title: Find the best products
steps.body: The problem. find only understands product codes, so AskMate says no to rimless toilet.
hints: This is Mission 4's best_dishes again, with products. Which products should a customer see if three of them score 2 and the rest score 1?

First make a list of what each of the customer's words means. Then a dict from each product's code to its score: max() of its values is the best score. Keep the products with that score, and sort them by price with sorted() and a key.

Nearly there: after the code part,  asked = [meaning(w) for w in words(question)]  ,  scores = {p["code"]: score(asked, p) for p in products}  ,  best = max(scores.values(), default=0)  ,  if best == 0: return []  ,  found = sorted((p for p in products if scores[p["code"]] == ____), key=lambda p: p["price"])  ,  return [p["code"] for p in found]

answer.why: Every product gets a score, and only the best ones are kept, so a product that matches one word never beats one that matches two. A best score of 0 means nothing matched, and an empty list makes AskMate say an honest no. Sorting by price shows the cheapest first.

steps.well_done: AskMate understands how people really ask.
steps.ask: Make find return the products that match the customer's words best, cheapest first.
steps.gets: the question, like "18 by 14 basin", and all 35 products
steps.gives: a list of product codes, like ["WBSN 277", "WBSN 278"], or an empty list when nothing matches
approach: Keep the product code part at the top: if the customer typed a code, that still wins.
Turn the question into words, and each word into its meaning: asked = [meaning(w) for w in words(question)].
Score every product and find the best score. If the best score is 0, nothing matched: return an empty list.
Keep every product with the best score, sort them by price, and return their codes.
steps.where: search.py, the function find. After it, decide answers if there is 1 product, asks which one if there are more, and says no if there are none.

steps.title: Boss Customer: the cheapest one
steps.body: A Boss Customer arrives. Vikram asks for the cheapest wall hung toilet. AskMate finds five and asks which one, but Vikram already said which: the cheapest.
hints: Your found list is sorted by price. Where in it is the cheapest product?
Just before the return, check if "cheapest" is in asked. If it is, keep only the first item of found with a slice.
Nearly there: before the return,  if "cheapest" in asked: found = found[:____]

answer.why: found is already cheapest first, so found[:1] is a list with only the cheapest product. One product means AskMate answers instead of asking.

steps.well_done: Vikram got his answer. Customers who tell you what they want should never be asked again.
steps.ask: When the customer says cheapest, give back only the cheapest product.
steps.gets: a question with the word cheapest, like "the cheapest wall hung toilet"
approach: Your list in find is already sorted cheapest first.
Just before the return, check if "cheapest" is one of the customer's words.
If it is, keep only the first product: the slice [:1] gives a list with just the first item.
steps.where: search.py, inside find, just before its last line.
